Project Overview

This project aimed to identify the most suitable locations for solar power plant development across Egypt by integrating GIS, Remote Sensing, and Machine Learning techniques. The workflow combined environmental, topographic, and infrastructure factors to generate a national-scale solar suitability model and support renewable energy planning.

The Challenge

Selecting locations for solar energy projects requires balancing multiple factors simultaneously, including solar radiation, terrain conditions, environmental restrictions, infrastructure accessibility, and population distribution. Traditional site selection methods often depend on subjective weighting and manual decision-making, introducing bias and reducing reliability.

The Objective

Develop an objective, data-driven framework capable of identifying optimal solar energy locations across Egypt using machine learning and geospatial analysis.

Data Sources Integrated:
Solar Radiation: ERA5-Land
Temperature: MODIS LST
Wind Speed: ERA5-Land
Topography: SRTM DEM, Slope, Aspect
Population Density: WorldPop
Protected Areas: WDPA Layers
Road Networks: OpenStreetMap
Electrical Grid: Infrastructure
Methodology & Machine Learning Workflow:
  1. Collect and prepare spatial datasets.
  2. Standardize coordinate systems (UTM Zone 36N) and raster resolutions.
  3. Clip and clean all layers for Egypt.
  4. Build a unified spatial database.
  5. Generate 2,000 training samples extracted from environmental & infrastructure datasets.
  6. Train a Random Forest classification model automatically learning relationships between variables.
  7. Apply the model nationwide across Egypt in Google Earth Engine.
  8. Produce a final 5-class suitability map (Unsuitable to Very Highly Suitable).
Results & Suitable Development Zones

Model Accuracy: 85–90%. Identified 5 top solar zones:

  • Aswan & Benban Solar Complex
  • East Oweinat
  • Gulf of Suez Corridor
  • Western Desert
  • Selected areas in Sinai
Strategic Key Findings
  • Western Desert: Emerged as one of the most promising regions due to high solar radiation, low population density, gentle terrain, and large available land areas.
  • Multi-Factor Feasibility: Solar radiation alone is not sufficient; infrastructure access, slope, population density, and environmental constraints significantly influence project feasibility.

Project Overview

This project evaluates the spatial efficiency and accessibility of secondary education services across Port Said Governorate using GIS and spatial statistics. The study investigates school distribution, service accessibility, educational gaps, population pressure, and social indicators to identify underserved areas and support evidence-based educational planning.

The Challenge

Port Said has experienced significant urban expansion and population growth, creating spatial imbalances between population concentrations and educational facilities. Central districts face overcrowding while peripheral districts suffer from severe accessibility gaps.

Study Area & Scope

Covered all 8 administrative districts of Port Said Governorate (Al-Zohour, Al-Manakh, Al-Arab, Al-Dawahi, Port Fouad, Al-Janoub, Al-Manasra, East Port Said) auditing 749,371 residents and 18,720 secondary-age students (15–19 years).

Data Sources Integrated:
School Database: 42 Secondary Schools
Demographics: CAPMAS Census Data
Education Data: Ministry EMIS Records
Spatial Data: HDX Boundaries & OSM
Advanced Spatial Statistics & GIS Workflow:
  1. Choropleth Distribution Analysis: Mapped school density across districts to identify spatial concentration vs deficiency zones.
  2. Average Nearest Neighbor (NNI): Evaluated spatial clustering, confirming a statistically significant clustered school distribution.
  3. 1000m Network Accessibility Buffer: Calculated service coverage zones around schools to pinpoint underserved communities.
  4. Population-to-School Ratio & Gap Analysis: Measured educational pressure (Students aged 15-19 ÷ Schools) to identify true supply shortages.
  5. Hotspot Analysis (Getis-Ord Gi*): Identified statistically significant school concentration Hotspots (Al-Zohour, Al-Manakh, Al-Arab) and Coldspots (Al-Janoub, Al-Manasra).
  6. Moran's I & GWR Modeling: Confirmed spatial autocorrelation and modeled Geographically Weighted Regression linking literacy rates to educational accessibility.
Key Statistical Findings
  • Clustered Distribution: NNI analysis proved schools are heavily clustered in urban cores rather than evenly spread.
  • Gi* Hotspots: Al-Zohour, Al-Manakh, Al-Arab form primary hotspots; Al-Janoub and Al-Manasra form significant coldspots.
  • Social Correlation: Districts with low school coverage exhibit higher illiteracy levels.
GIS Recommendations
  • Establish new secondary schools in underserved Al-Janoub and Al-Manasra districts.
  • Reduce overcrowding in Al-Zohour, Al-Manakh, and Al-Arab.
  • Implement periodic GIS educational accessibility assessments.

Project Overview

This project investigates the development potential of the Qattara Depression in Egypt’s Western Desert through an integrated geospatial and environmental assessment framework combining Remote Sensing, GIS, Machine Learning, Morphometric Analysis, Climatic Modeling, and Spatial Decision Support.

The Challenge

The Qattara Depression (~19,500 km², lowest point -133m below sea level) lacks research integrating geomorphology, climate dynamics, environmental change, hydrology, and AI spatial decision-support into a unified strategic development framework.

4 Random Forest AI Models
  • Geomorphological RF: 98.78% Accuracy
  • Environmental RF: 98.64% Accuracy
  • Hazard & Water Flow RF: 100.00% Accuracy
  • Development Suitability RF: 99.73% Accuracy
Data Sources Integrated:
Terrain: SRTM DEM (30m)
Climate Data: ERA5 Rain, Temp & Wind
MODIS Data: ET, NDVI, BSI, SAVI, SI
Geology: Faults & Lithological Maps
Key Findings & Technical Breakthroughs:
  • 25%–35% High Development Suitability: Identified ~4,900–6,800 km² of stable flat alluvial plains suitable for agriculture and urban expansion.
  • Water Transfer Feasibility: Natural terrain supports water movement; major flow accumulation zones exist naturally, proving extensive artificial canals are not required. Northeastern margin identified as optimal intake location.
  • Environmental Dynamics: LST and evapotranspiration show warming trends, but sustainable water management guarantees long-term viability.

Project Overview

This project analyzes the spatiotemporal evolution of agricultural land in Farafra Depression, Western Desert of Egypt, between 1990 and 2024. The study integrates Remote Sensing, GIS, Google Earth Engine, and Artificial Intelligence techniques to monitor agricultural expansion and identify newly reclaimed lands in one of Egypt’s key desert development regions.

The Challenge

Egypt relies on desert reclamation to support food security. Monitoring multi-decadal expansion across vast arid regions requires processing large multi-temporal satellite imagery collections and accurately extracting vegetation spectral indices.

34-Year Growth Evolution
  • 1990: 12.87 km²
  • 2000: 38.42 km²
  • 2010: 121.70 km²
  • 2015: 214.70 km²
  • 2020: 356.90 km²
  • 2024: 535.10 km² (+4,058% Total Growth!)
Datasets & Spectral Indices:
Landsat 5 TM: 1990 Image Baseline
Landsat 7 ETM+: 2000 & 2010 Time Series
Landsat 8 OLI: 2015, 2020 & 2024 Series
Spectral Indices: NDVI, SAVI, NDWI, EVI
Major Findings & Drivers:
  • Rapid Post-2015 Acceleration: Most new agricultural reclamation occurred after 2015, concentrated in northern and northeastern parts of Farafra Depression.
  • Technology & Groundwater Drivers: Expansion was driven primarily by groundwater availability and center-pivot irrigation systems.
  • Random Forest AI Precision: Achieved high classification performance separating crops from desert sand using multi-spectral indices.

Project Overview

This project investigates the spatial relationship between healthcare service distribution and endemic disease prevalence within Belqas District, Dakahlia Governorate, Egypt. Using GIS, the study evaluates healthcare accessibility, service coverage, and disease distribution patterns to identify underserved areas and support evidence-based healthcare planning.

The Challenge

Healthcare facilities are concentrated in urban hubs while peripheral rural villages face limited accessibility. The study answered whether healthcare services spatially align with population needs and how disease prevalence relates to travel accessibility.

12 Disease Categories Analyzed

Hepatitis (A, B, C), Bilharzia, Intestinal Parasites, Hypertension, Diabetes, Heart Diseases, Kidney Failure, Anemia, Asthma, Pneumonia, Skin Diseases, Gastrointestinal Diseases.

Data Sources Integrated:
Healthcare Data: Hospitals, Rural Units, Clinics
Socioeconomic Data: CAPMAS Demographics
Health Directorate: Dakahlia Health Records
Environmental Data: LULC, Road Net, Waste Sites
Priority Locations for Hospital Expansion:
  1. Area between El-Sharkia and El-Samaha Al-Kobra: High rural population density with severe travel time deficit.
  2. Southern Expansion Zone of Belqas City: Rapidly growing urban perimeter under high medical capacity pressure.
  3. Al-Hafeer & Al-Amal Region near Qalabsho: Agricultural zone with high endemic disease prevalence and extreme distance from hospital hubs.
